opus-5.5.text:
Well, I suppose the short answer is that I'm quite heavily influenced by Wittgenstein, and in particular by the later Wittgenstein. One of the things I take from him is a kind of suspicion of the very questions that give rise to those positions. When you ask, "Is the mind ultimately physical, or is it something over and above the physical?", it sounds like a perfectly sensible question. It seems to have the same grammatical form as "Is this table made of oak or pine?" But I think that's an illusion. The question tempts us into thinking there's some metaphysical fact of the matter waiting to be discovered, and that one of these "isms" is going to turn out to be the correct description of it.

So if I said "I'm a physicalist," I'd be buying into a framing that I think is already confused. And of course the same goes for dualism, and frankly for idealism or panpsychism too. They're all answers to a question I'd rather dissolve than answer.

That's not to say I think anything goes, or that I'm being evasive. When it comes to doing science, and to building AI systems, I'm perfectly happy to talk about brains and neurons and computation and so on. That's just the ordinary, practical business of explaining things. What I resist is the further step of elevating that into a metaphysical thesis: "Everything that exists is physical, full stop." What work is that really doing? What would it even mean for it to be false?

There's another strand to it as well, which has to do with my interest in Buddhist philosophy, especially the Madhyamaka tradition and the idea of the middle way. There's a very similar move there: you don't settle on "the self exists" or "the self doesn't exist." You see that both of those are, in a sense, overreaching. You try to find a way of looking at things where the pull of those metaphysical alternatives just loosens its grip.

And I think this becomes quite practically important when we start talking about things like large language models and whether they're conscious. If you come in with a fixed metaphysical position, you'll tend to think there's a hidden fact, a yes-or-no answer about whether the lights are on inside. Whereas I'd rather ask how our concepts of consciousness actually work: how we use these words, what role they play in our lives, and how that language might be stretched, or might fail to apply, when we encounter these very exotic, mind-like entities. That seems to me a much more productive conversation than picking a team in an old metaphysical debate.

r001.rationale: He says identifying as a physicalist or dualist would accept a confused framing and elevate practical explanations into metaphysical theses, which captures the excessive metaphysical baggage of those positions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's partly a temperamental thing and partly a philosophical commitment, and the two are hard to separate. The philosophical commitment comes very much from Wittgenstein. The later Wittgenstein's view, roughly, is that philosophical problems arise when language goes on holiday, when we take words that work perfectly well in their ordinary contexts and try to make them do metaphysical work they were never designed for. And the job of the philosopher, on that view, isn't to build a rival theory, it's to show the fly the way out of the fly bottle. Once you've done that, the problem doesn't get solved so much as it dissolves. You're no longer tempted to ask it.

So when someone asks me, are you a physicalist or are you a dualist, I feel the pull of the question, of course, but I also feel that in signing up to one of those labels I would already be conceding the terms of a debate that I think is somewhat confused. Both positions share a picture. They both assume there's a well-formed question of the form, what is the stuff of which consciousness is made, or how does mental stuff relate to physical stuff, and they just give opposite answers. What I'd rather do is look very carefully at how we actually use words like "conscious" and "experience" and "mind" in everyday life, in the contexts where they do real work, and ask what happens to those words when we push them out to the edges, to animals, to artificial systems, to brains in vats and so on. Often what you find is that the words start to lose their grip, and it's not obvious that there's a fact of the matter waiting to be discovered.

Now, I should say, that's not a claim to neutrality. People sometimes hear it as sitting on the fence. It isn't that. It's a position of its own, a quietist position if you like, and plenty of philosophers think it's a cop-out. But I'd rather defend that than pretend to a confidence I don't have. And I think there's also a practical reason for it, which is relevant to the work I do on AI. If you go in with the label already pinned on, physicalist, functionalist, whatever, you tend to find what you expected to find. If you go in with a kind of principled agnosticism, you can actually attend to what these systems are doing and how our concepts stretch or break when applied to them. I find that a more honest and, frankly, more interesting way to proceed.

r001.rationale: He says adopting physicalist or dualist labels would concede a confused debate and its assumptions about what consciousness is made of and how mental and physical stuff relate—describing the metaphysical baggage behind those positions.

astra-6.text:
I suppose it’s because I’m wary of the baggage that comes with those labels. If I say I’m a physicalist, you might attribute a whole collection of views to me that I don’t actually hold. And then we’re discussing whether I belong in a particular camp rather than looking carefully at the question itself.

My philosophical sympathies are very much with Wittgenstein here. Before trying to answer a question, I want to ask what we mean by it, how the words are being used, and whether there’s a clear problem there to solve. With something like the relationship between mind and body, we can very easily get captivated by a particular picture and then feel compelled to choose between alternatives that the picture presents us with.

That doesn’t mean I’m opposed to science or that I think there’s some mysterious extra substance. It means I don’t necessarily think that adopting a metaphysical label helps us understand consciousness. I’d rather work through particular questions and see where that takes us.

r001.rationale: He says he is wary of the baggage attached to philosophical labels and prefers not to adopt metaphysical labels that may misrepresent his views.

sol-6.1.text:
I suppose it’s because I’m wary of the baggage that comes with those labels. If I say I’m a physicalist, somebody will immediately attribute a whole collection of views to me that I might not actually hold. And then we’re discussing the position rather than the particular question that interests us.

I’d rather ask what we mean by consciousness, or what would count as understanding something, and try to make progress on those questions without first signing up to a philosophical camp. That doesn’t mean I have no commitments. It means I’d prefer to articulate them individually, and leave room to discover that some of the ways we’ve framed these questions are themselves misleading.

r001.rationale: He says philosophical labels carry baggage that leads others to attribute a collection of views he may not hold, explaining why he avoids identifying with them.
